title: A nondifferential operator whose every higher power is differential
notes: Gelfand states that there is an operator whose second, third and all subsequent powers are differential operators, although the first is not.
statement: Interpret operator in the ring of formal pseudodifferential operators over \(\mathbb C(x)\). Set \(P=D^2-2/x^2\), \(R=D^3-3x^{-2}D+3x^{-3}\). They commute and satisfy \(R^2=P^3\). Hence \(Q=RP^{-1}\) obeys \(Q^2=P\), \(Q^3=R\); since every integer at least two is a nonnegative combination of two and three, all \(Q^m\), \(m\ge2\), are differential. But \(Q\) is not differential: its order and leading coefficient would force \(Q=D+a\), and comparison of the \(D\)-coefficient in \(Q^2=P\) gives \(a=0\), a contradiction. The same example works with smooth germs near any nonzero point.
reconstruction: \oursComputed\ The rational degeneration and algebraic verification supply a precise example; the source does not specify the operator category or display the example. This is a verification of classical formulas, not a new existence result.
fate: \citet[\S3, equations (2)--(3), and \S4]{mulase1990geometric} gives the commuting family and formal fractional-power framework.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: The gap count recalled in residue-class form
notes: The least nongap \(n\), the integers \(\mu_i\), their sum \(g\), and the existence of exactly \(g\) missing pole orders are repeated.
statement: For a smooth connected projective complex curve of genus \(g\) and a point \(P\), the pole-order semigroup has \(g\) positive gaps. With \(n\) its least positive element and \(i+\mu_i n\) the least element in residue class \(i\), the count is \(g=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\mu_i\), as in 1975-383.3. This is a statement about functions having no poles away from \(P\), not about unrestricted meromorphic functions.
reconstruction: The sole-pole condition is made explicit; the equivalence follows by counting each residue class.
fate: This repeats the classical gap theory discussed above; \citet[Ch.~II]{forster1981riemann}.

title: The reciprocal polar coefficient of the connection
notes: After choosing a local frame \(e\), the notes write \(\nabla e/e=1/(b_0z)+\cdots\), where \(b_0\) is the leading coefficient of the homomorphism.
statement: Fix the curve coordinate \(z\), and a local generator \(e\) of \(L\) near \(P\). If \(\nabla e=(b_0^{-1}z^{-1}+O(1))e\), \(b_0\in B^*\), then the principal-part datum is \(\beta=b_0^{-1}[z^{-1}]\). Multiplication by \(z^{-m}\) on the associated graded corresponds to \(b_0^m\nabla^m\), giving leading coefficient \(b_0^m\) for the operator attached to a normalized pole of order \(m\). A regular change of frame contributes only a regular logarithmic-derivative term.

title: Initial value and leading coefficient in the rank-one inverse correspondence
notes: The theorem is abbreviated to a point of the Jacobian in general position. The construction then uses a natural map \(B\to\mathbb C\), value at zero, to obtain \(L_0\).
statement: For \(B\) the algebra of smooth complex-valued germs at zero, evaluation \(B\to\mathbb C\) pulls the family back to its initial line bundle \(L_0\). Fixing a unit leading-coefficient germ \(b_0\), the gauge classes are parametrized by acyclic \(L_0\in\operatorname{Pic}^{g-1}(X)\). If \(b_0\) is not fixed, it is additional data and the Jacobian point alone is insufficient. For an arbitrary differential algebra \(B\), neither evaluation at zero nor this initial-value classification is automatic.
reconstruction: The opening general differential-algebra notation is narrowed to the germ setting when evaluation and uniqueness of the path are invoked.
fate: \citet[Corollary 2]{drinfeld1977commutative} states both pieces of data explicitly.

title: The Picard group and the tangent space of the Jacobian
notes: The tangent space is identified with \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\), but the notes identify the whole Jacobian with \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X^*)\).
statement: For a smooth compact connected complex curve, \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X^*)=\operatorname{Pic}(X)\) includes all integer degrees. Its identity component is \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)=\operatorname{Jac}(X)\). The analytic exponential sequence gives \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)\cong H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)/\operatorname{im}H^1(X,\mathbb Z)\), with the conventional \(2\pi i\) factor according to the chosen exponential. Its tangent space at the identity, and by translation at any point, is \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\). A fixed-degree Picard variety is a torsor for this group.
reconstruction: The missing degree-zero qualification is corrected; removing the star is interpreted as linearizing transition functions, not as a literal cohomology operation.
fate: The tangent-space identification is used in \citet[Corollary 2, proof]{drinfeld1977commutative}; the surrounding Picard theory is classical.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, the result is established in the stated scope.

title: The principal-part boundary map gives the Jacobian velocity
notes: The class of \(1/z\) under the boundary map from \(\mathcal O_X(P)/\mathcal O_X\) is denoted \(\eta_P\), and \(\ell^{\prime}(x)=\eta_P/b_0(x)\). The final explanation identifies its line with the tangent to the Abel image of the curve.
statement: Let \(\delta_P:H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(P)/\mathcal O_X)\to H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\) be the connecting homomorphism and put \(\eta_P=\delta_P([z^{-1}])\). For the smooth-germ rank-one data above, choose the Cech and divisor sign conventions consistently. The corresponding Picard path satisfies \(\ell^{\prime}(x)=b_0(x)^{-1}\eta_P\), hence locally \(\ell(x)=\ell(0)+\eta_P\int_0^x b_0(s)^{-1}\,ds\) in a lift to the universal cover. For \(g\ge1\), the line spanned by \(\eta_P\) is the tangent image of \(X\to\operatorname{Jac}(X)\), \(Q\mapsto[Q-P]\); a chosen tangent coordinate fixes its scale and convention fixes its sign. For genus zero the Jacobian and this vector vanish.
reconstruction: \oursComputed\ Integrating the stated velocity gives the displayed local lift. The genus-zero exception and sign convention are explicit reconstruction; no new flow theorem is claimed.
fate: \citet[Corollary 2, proof]{drinfeld1977commutative} identifies the derivative with the boundary image of the principal part.

title: Yang–Mills potentials, curvature and action
notes:
The notes take traceless anti-Hermitian \(2	imes2\) matrices \(A_\mu\), write \(A_\mu\in SU(2)\) followed by ``Lie algebra'', and define \(F_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu+g[A_\mu,A_

statement: A connection on a trivial \(SU(2)\)-bundle is a one-form \(A=A_\mu dx^\mu\) with \(A_\mu\in\mathfrak{su}(2)\). Its curvature is \(F=dA+gA\wedge A\). Use the positive invariant inner product \(\langle X,Y\rangle=-\operatorname{tr}(XY)\) on the Lie algebra. The Euclidean action is \(S_E=\frac14\int\langle F_{\mu\nu},F_{\mu\nu}\rangle\,d^4x\); Lorentzian contraction instead uses the spacetime metric.
fate: These are the classical definitions; see \citet[Section 1]{jaffewitten2000yangmills}. The source's positive trace formula and anti-Hermitian convention cannot both give a nonnegative Euclidean action.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Legendre transformation and Gauss constraint
notes: The notes set \(e_i=\dot A_i-D_iA_0\), observe the absence of \(\dot A_0\), and introduce \(h_i=\frac12\varepsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}\). Both displayed Hamiltonians put a factor \(1/2\) on the \(A_0\)-term.
statement:
With \(L=\frac12\int(\langle e,e\rangle-\langle h,h\rangle)\), the canonical momenta are \(e_i\) and \(e_0=0\). Integration by parts, with boundary terms zero, gives
\[H=\frac12\int(\langle e,e\rangle+\langle h,h\rangle)\,d^3x-\int\langle A_0,D_ie_i\rangle\,d^3x.\]
Variation in \(A_0\) imposes \(D_ie_i=0\). The coefficient of this last term is one, with the conventions just fixed.
reconstruction: \ours\ The displayed result follows directly from \(\dot A=e+DA_0\). A positive Lie-algebra inner product replaces the ambiguous bare trace. No global Hamiltonian phase space is asserted without boundary and function-space choices.
fate: Canonical constraint reduction predates the seminar: \citet[abstract]{arnowittfickler1962quantization}; the reconstructed Hamiltonian also agrees with \citet[Section 2, equations (1)--(5)]{reinhardt2018coulomb}. The 1962 paper's metadata and abstract, rather than its full derivation, were accessible.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Propagation of the Gauss constraint
notes: The speaker asks whether \(D_ie_i=0\) continues to hold and writes a Poisson-bracket condition for \(\rho=D_ie_i\).
statement: On the canonical phase space, set \(G(\omega)=\int\langle\omega,D_ie_i\rangle\). The gauge-invariant reduced Hamiltonian \(H_0=\frac12\int(e^2+h^2)\) obeys \(\{G(\omega),H_0\}=0\). Consequently Gauss's constraint propagates in temporal gauge; with an arbitrary multiplier \(A_0\), its evolution is an adjoint rotation and preserves the zero constraint surface.
reconstruction: \ours\ The source's bracket is the negative of the convention \(\{A_i,e_j\}=\delta_{ij}\delta\), although its Hamilton equations use that latter convention. The vanishing assertion is unaffected; the sign must be fixed when generating gauge transformations.
fate: This is part of the pre-existing first-order canonical formulation; \citet[abstract, discussion of constraint conservation]{arnowittfickler1962quantization}. The proof here is the elementary implication of gauge invariance, not an attribution of a newly announced theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Gauge covariance and transverse coordinates
notes: The transformation \(A_i^\Omega=\Omega^{-1}A_i\Omega+g^{-1}\Omega^{-1}\partial_i\Omega\) preserves \(\operatorname{tr}h^2\). The notes then write every field in terms of \(a_i\) with \(\partial_i a_i=0\) and a gauge matrix.
statement: For smooth \(\Omega:\mathbb R^3\to SU(2)\), \(F_{ij}^\Omega=\Omega^{-1}F_{ij}\Omega\), so the magnetic energy is gauge invariant. Coulomb gauge \(\partial_i a_i=0\) is a local slice where its linearization \(M=-\partial_iD_i(a)\) is invertible after boundary conditions and residual constant transformations are fixed.
reconstruction: A local slice, not a globally unique decomposition, is the justified reading. Distinct gauge-equivalent transverse fields may exist.
fate: The Coulomb formulation remains useful, with its gauge-fixing determinant and Gribov restriction made explicit in \citet[Section 2]{reinhardt2018coulomb}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Longitudinal electric field and the Coulomb kernel
notes: The notes split \(e_i=P_i+\partial_i\Psi\), \(\partial_iP_i=0\), and call the longitudinal energy Coulomb energy. The commutator on the right of the Gauss equation changes order twice.
statement:
Fix \(D_i=\partial_i+g[a_i,\cdot]\) and \(D_ie_i=\rho\). Then
\[D_i\partial_i\Psi=\rho-g[a_i,P_i]=:\rho_{\rm tot}.\]
For transverse \(a\), \(M=-\partial D=-D\partial\), so \(\Psi=-M^{-1}\rho_{\rm tot}\) and
\[H_C=\tfrac12\langle\rho_{\rm tot},M^{-1}(-\Delta)M^{-1}\rho_{\rm tot}\rangle\]
when \(M\) is self-adjoint and invertible on the chosen domain. The cross term \(\int P_i\partial_i\Psi\) vanishes by integration by parts.
reconstruction: \ours\ The sign is forced by the source's definitions, rather than chosen to imitate a later convention for the gluonic charge. The notes omit \(g\) in the first version and reverse the bracket in the later versions.
fate: The source explicitly credits Schwinger. His 1962 radiation-gauge paper is an identified historical match at abstract level; the modern kernel is displayed in \citet[Section 2, equation (5)]{reinhardt2018coulomb}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Recovery of the Abelian Coulomb energy
notes: For \(g=0\) the notes write \(\Delta\Psi=\rho\) and identify the energy with a double integral having kernel \(1/|x-y|\).
statement:
For a sufficiently decaying smooth charge on \(\mathbb R^3\), \(\Psi(x)=-\int\rho(y)/(4\pi|x-y|)\,dy\) solves \(\Delta\Psi=\rho\). Thus
\[\tfrac12\int|\nabla\Psi|^2\,dx=\tfrac1{8\pi}\iint\frac{\rho(x)\rho(y)}{|x-y|}\,dx\,dy.\]
Point charges require subtraction or regularization of divergent self energies.
reconstruction: \ours\ This is an explicit reconstruction using \(-\Delta(4\pi|x|)^{-1}=\delta_0\); the notebook suppresses normalization constants. It follows directly by Green's identity.
fate: The elementary electrostatic calculation supplies the exact normalization behind the source formula.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Perturbation of the non-Abelian Gauss equation
notes: An inverse-Laplacian expansion and diagrams with zero, one and two insertions of \(a_i\) are written; the first correction contains no \(g\). The accompanying historical remark names Khriplovich and Gross.
statement:
For \(P=0\), formally write \(L_a\Psi=\sum_i[a_i,\partial_i\Psi]\). Then
\[(\Delta+gL_a)^{-1}\rho=\Delta^{-1}\rho-g\Delta^{-1}L_a\Delta^{-1}\rho+O(g^2).\]
For \(P\ne0\) one must also expand the source \(\rho-g[a_i,P_i]\). Analytic convergence requires an operator topology in which \(\|g\Delta^{-1}L_a\|<1\); no such estimate is supplied.
reconstruction: \ours\ This is the formal Neumann expansion of the preceding reconstructed equation. The list of physicists does not by itself specify a beta function, renormalization scheme, or an asymptotic-freedom theorem.
fate: Schwinger's pre-existing Coulomb-gauge program is identifiable \citep[abstract]{schwinger1962relativistic}; the particular omitted perturbative calculation attributed to Khriplovich and Gross is not identifiable from this page.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Canonical quantization in Coulomb gauge
notes: The commutator is abbreviated as \([a(x),p(y)]=\delta(x-y)\).
statement:
For transverse components, the formal equal-time relation is
\[[a_i^a(x),P_j^b(y)]=i\hbar\delta^{ab}\left(\delta_{ij}-\frac{\partial_i\partial_j}{\Delta}\right)\delta(x-y).\]
A quantum Hamiltonian further requires regularization, ordering and the gauge-fixed inner product. The formula alone is not a construction of continuum Yang--Mills theory.
fate: The Schrödinger representation and the Faddeev--Popov density are described in \citet[Section 2]{reinhardt2018coulomb}. The transverse projector is forced by \(\partial_i a_i=\partial_iP_i=0\).
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Vacuum averaging of the charge interaction
notes: The kernel \(F(x,y,a)\) replaces \(1/|x-y|\), and \(\delta E=\int\rho(x)\langle F(x,y,a)\rangle\rho(y)\,dx\,dy\) is proposed.
statement: For specified external color sources, a regulated Coulomb-gauge vacuum expectation of \(M^{-1}(-\Delta)M^{-1}\) defines an instantaneous color-Coulomb contribution. Whether the full static-source ground-state energy grows linearly at large separation is the confinement question, not a consequence of taking this expectation.
fate: The approach has a substantial later literature; \citet[Sections 2--3]{reinhardt2018coulomb}. The relation to confinement requires separating instantaneous energy from the fully relaxed static potential; \citet[Section 5]{jaffewitten2000yangmills} distinguishes confinement from the Yang--Mills existence and mass-gap problem.
present_status: As of November 2026, this fragment supplies a formal route to the confinement problem GP-1975-10, not its solution. The notes specify neither a regulated vacuum nor a limiting construction.
worth: A precise comparison between the instantaneous Coulomb kernel and gauge-invariant static energy remains useful for understanding what this calculation can establish.

title: The generalized Poisson distribution
notes: For \(0\leq\alpha<1\), \(P_n=e^{-x_0-\alpha n}x_0(x_0+\alpha n)^{n-1}/n!\); at \(\alpha=0\) the distribution is Poisson.
statement: Let \(x_0>0\), \(0\leq\alpha<1\), and \(n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). Set \(P_0=e^{-x_0}\) and use the displayed formula for \(n\ge1\). These numbers are nonnegative. The parameter range avoids the finite-support difficulties of negative deformation parameters.
fate: This matches \citet[Section 3, equation (3.1)]{consuljain1973poisson}, received in May 1971, revised in October 1972 and published in November 1973. The biological provenance in this intervention remains unspecified.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Normalization of the generalized Poisson law
notes: The explicit exercise is to verify \(\sum_{n\ge0}P_n=1\).
statement:
Let \(T(z)\) be the nonnegative solution near zero of \(T=z\exp(\alpha(T-1))\). Lagrange inversion gives
\[\sum_{n\ge0}P_nz^n=\exp(x_0(T(z)-1)).\]
For \(0\leq\alpha<1\), continuity from below and the minimal fixed point at \(z=1\) give \(T(1)=1\), hence total mass one.
reconstruction: \ours\ The generating-function proof is supplied here. For \(\alpha=0\), \(T=z\). For \(0<\alpha<1\), the function \(h(t)=e^{\alpha(t-1)}-t\) has \(h(1)=0\) and \(h'(t)=\alpha e^{\alpha(t-1)}-1<0\) on \([0,1]\), so it has no fixed-point zero below one. Monotone iteration from zero for \(0\le z\le1\) identifies the nonnegative branch and its limit.
fate: Normalization belongs to the already published distribution \citep[Sections 2--3]{consuljain1973poisson}. Thus this is an expository exercise, not a problem first solved after the seminar.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: The first Brauer–Thrall theorem
notes: A finite-dimensional algebra has either finitely many indecomposable modules or indecomposables of arbitrarily large dimension. Roiter is named, followed by an Auslander generalization to Artinian rings.
statement: For a finite-dimensional algebra \(\Lambda\) over a field, bounded dimensions of finite-dimensional indecomposable modules imply that there are only finitely many isomorphism classes of such modules. The corresponding formulation for Artin algebras uses composition length. The phrase ``Artinian rings'' needs the precise finiteness setting of the theorem being invoked.
fate: Roiter's article was submitted on 20 March 1968 and published that year \citep{roiter1968brauerthrall}. A later proof within Artin-algebra representation theory is given by \citet[Section 6]{ringel2006foundation}; no claim about arbitrary left Artinian rings is inferred from that proof.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Infinite chains of indecomposable modules
notes: The notebook asks for or asserts an infinite chain \(A_1\subset A_2\subset\cdots\) with indecomposable terms in the infinite case.
statement: If an Artin algebra is of infinite representation type, there is an infinite sequence of finite-length indecomposables and proper monomorphisms \(M_1\hookrightarrow M_2\hookrightarrow\cdots\). The chain can be chosen to consist of Gabriel--Roiter inclusions; its lengths are unbounded.
fate: A precise strengthened form is \citet[Section 7.3, Theorem]{ringel2006foundation}, published in 2006 after lectures in 2003--2005. The source does not specify the inclusions, and its exact contemporary publication was not identified.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Bounding composition length by indecomposable-chain length
notes: Besides composition length \(\ell(M)\), the notes define \(\bar\ell(M)\) as the largest number of terms in a chain of indecomposable submodules. Their quantifier order is \(\forall N\,\exists n:\bar\ell(M)\le n\Rightarrow\ell(M)\le N\).
statement: The substantive uniform bound is: for each Artin algebra \(\Lambda\) and each \(n\), there exists \(N(\Lambda,n)\) such that \(\bar\ell(M)\le n\) implies \(\ell(M)\le N(\Lambda,n)\), for indecomposable finite-length \(M\). If \(p,q\) are the maximum lengths of indecomposable projectives and injectives, one may take \(N=(pq)^{n-1}\): a Gabriel--Roiter filtration starts with a simple module, and each inclusion multiplies length by at most \(pq\).
reconstruction: \ours\ The implication printed in the notes is not this bound; it is too weak to express the intended control. The exponent is a direct deduction from the cited filtration and inclusion bound, not a formula attributed to the notebook.
fate: Use \citet[Section 1.5 and Section 3.1, Corollary]{ringel2006foundation}. These establish the ingredients in the Artin-algebra setting; this is a later rigorous match to the intended estimate, not an exact identification of Roiter's wording.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Integral forms and finite or affine Dynkin diagrams
notes: The form \(q(x)=\sum a_ix_i^2+\sum_{i<j}b_{ij}x_ix_j\) has \(a_i>0\), \(b_{ij}\le0\), and \(a_i\mid b_{ij}\). Positivity is associated with Dynkin diagrams; nonnegativity with extended diagrams. Kirillov draws the finite families.
statement: Assume integer coefficients, divisibility at both endpoints, and connected coefficient graph. The matrix \(C_{ii}=2\), \(C_{ij}=b_{ij}/a_i\) is a symmetrizable generalized Cartan matrix. Positive definiteness gives finite type; positive semidefiniteness with a nontrivial radical gives affine type. Nonnegativity alone includes finite type, and disconnected forms require a componentwise statement.
reconstruction: Connectedness and singularity distinguish the affine assertion. The cited source directly treats the simply laced representation-theoretic part; the Cartan-matrix translation of the displayed form is an explicit reconstruction.
fate: The simply laced correspondence and its use in quiver classification predate the meeting: \citet[Section 3]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}. This connects thematically to GP-1972-301 and GP-1972-302, but no repeated quiver-classification question is written here. The nonsimply-laced integral-form conditions and the connected nonnegative case are addressed in \citet[Section 1 and Lemma 6]{roiter1978roots}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.
speaker: A. V. Roiter; A. A. Kirillov (intervention)

title: Reflections and roots of simply laced forms
notes: A reflection changes one coordinate and preserves \(q\); roots are obtained from coordinate vectors. In the equal-coefficient case, \(q(x)=1\) is the root criterion.
statement: For \(a_i=1\), define \(s_i(x)=x-(2x_i+\sum_{j\ne i}b_{ij}x_j)e_i\). For a finite simply laced Dynkin form, the integral solutions of \(q(x)=1\) are precisely the real roots \(\{w(e_i):w\in\langle s_1,\ldots,s_n\rangle\}\). In affine type the same norm condition characterizes real roots; nonzero imaginary roots have \(q=0\) and must be listed separately.
fate: The finite-type reflection argument is already in \citet[Section 3]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}. The word ``roots'' in the notes is orbit-defined, and should not silently be enlarged to all imaginary roots. The affine norm criterion also follows from \citet[Proposition 4]{roiter1978roots}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: A divisibility criterion for roots
notes: For the more general form, the notebook states that \(x\) is a root if and only if \(q(x)\) divides every \(a_ix_i\).
statement: Let \(q=\sum_i a_ix_i^2+\sum_{i<j}b_{ij}x_ix_j\) have positive integral \(a_i\), nonpositive \(b_{ij}\), and \(a_i,a_j\mid b_{ij}\). Assume its connected diagram is finite or affine Dynkin. A vector \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\) is a real root, that is an orbit of a coordinate vector under the integral reflections, if and only if \(q(x)>0\) and \(q(x)\mid a_ix_i\) for every \(i\). The positivity condition excludes the radical in affine type. This criterion does not hold without restrictions for arbitrary indefinite forms.
reconstruction: Finite or connected affine type is supplied from the surrounding discussion, and \(q(x)>0\) is made explicit. A later star-shaped example with five or more arms is indefinite and must not inherit this criterion automatically.
fate: An exact source is \citet[Proposition 4, p.205; Lemma 6, p.206]{roiter1978roots}. Roiter proves the criterion when every proper coordinate restriction is positive; the finite and connected affine cases satisfy this hypothesis. Russian publication was in 1978, English translation in 1980. The notebook of 22 March 1976 is an earlier verified witness to this claim.
present_status: As of November 2026, the stated finite/connected affine criterion is established. The initial source-identification gap was resolved by the 1978 article; indefinite extensions require its further hypotheses.

title: Roots of the star-shaped quadratic form
notes: The final example is \(q=x_0^2+\cdots+x_n^2-x_0(x_1+\cdots+x_n)\); the question is to obtain all roots by elementary reflections, illustrated by a word-changing analogy.
statement: The orbit of the coordinate vectors under the reflections attached to this star is a precise enumerable set of real roots. Completing squares gives \(q=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-x_0/2)^2+(1-n/4)x_0^2\): the cases \(n\le3\) are finite, \(n=4\) is affine \(\widetilde D_4\), and \(n\ge5\) is indefinite. An exhaustive finite list is therefore not an appropriate interpretation for all \(n\).
reconstruction: \ours\ The square completion and the distinction between finite enumeration and an orbit algorithm are supplied here. The notes do not state a bound on word length or demand an algorithm deciding all imaginary roots.
fate: The reflection machinery is already available in \citet[Sections 2--3]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}. This question is understood as an exercise in that machinery; no separate unresolved classification conjecture is inferred.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Superfunctions and split supermanifolds
notes: Functions depend smoothly on commuting variables \(x\) and polynomially on anticommuting variables \(\xi\). A vector-bundle description is attributed to Rudakov.
statement: A smooth real supermanifold of dimension \(p|q\) is a locally ringed space locally isomorphic to \((U,C^\infty_U\otimes\Lambda^\bullet\mathbb R^q)\). A split example is \((M,\Gamma(\Lambda E^*))\) for a rank-\(q\) vector bundle \(E\to M\). The local model does not itself select a canonical global splitting.
fate: The sheaf definition was published by \citet[pp. 505--506]{berezinleites1975supermanifolds} in 1975, following submission on 24 March 1975. The attribution to Rudakov is preserved as the seminar's attribution, without inferring a separate publication.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Berezin integration
notes: Integration is specified by \(\int d\xi=0\) and \(\int\xi,d\xi=1\), extending to products of anticommuting variables.
statement: For an ordered set of odd generators, Berezin integration is coefficient extraction: \(\int d\xi_q\cdots d\xi_1\,f\) is the coefficient of \(\xi_1\cdots\xi_q\). Changing the order changes signs. On a supermanifold, coordinate-invariant integration requires the Berezinian transformation law, rather than an ordinary volume form.
fate: The integration framework predates this meeting; see \citet[Section 5]{berezinkac1970lie} and \citet[pp. 507--508]{berezinleites1975supermanifolds}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Coordinate changes with nilpotent terms
notes: The examples include changes of an even coordinate by a product of odd coordinates, such as \(x\mapsto x+\xi_1\xi_2\), as well as transformations of the odd variables.
statement: A morphism is determined locally by parity-preserving substitutions: even coordinates are sent to even superfunctions and odd coordinates to odd ones. A local isomorphism requires invertibility of the ordinary even Jacobian and of the linear odd part after nilpotents are discarded.
fate: These are the local morphisms in the sheaf-theoretic construction of \citet[pp. 505--506]{berezinleites1975supermanifolds}. Nilpotent corrections explain why a bundle picture does not exhaust the coordinate transformations.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: An unnamed 64-dimensional algebra
notes: The notes mention a 64-dimensional algebra that is said to describe particles better than \(SU(3)\), without naming its generators or representation.
statement: Dimension alone does not determine a Lie superalgebra, its parity dimensions, real form, representation or physical model. No definite mathematical identification follows.
fate: Targeted searches on Berezin, Kirillov, 64-dimensional superalgebras and particle models did not identify a source matching all of these details.
present_status: As of November 2026, this remains an unresolved identification in the historical record.

title: Lie superalgebras and associative envelopes
notes: The bracket is graded skew-symmetric, satisfies graded Jacobi, and is obtained from multiplication by a signed commutator; a converse is mentioned.
statement: Over a field of characteristic zero, a Lie superalgebra \(\mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_0\oplus\mathfrak g_1\) satisfies \([x,y]=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[y,x]\) and the graded Jacobi identity. Every associative superalgebra has this bracket. Conversely \(\mathfrak g\) embeds in its universal enveloping superalgebra, whose associated graded algebra is \(S(\mathfrak g_0)\otimes\Lambda(\mathfrak g_1)\).
reconstruction: The precise converse is an enveloping-algebra statement, not an assertion that every Lie superalgebra already has an associative multiplication on its own vector space.
fate: The definitions and representation framework are present in \citet[Sections 3--4]{berezinkac1970lie}, published in 1970. The enveloping formulation spells out the otherwise ambiguous converse.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: The formal Lie correspondence in supergeometry
notes: A ``Lie theorem'' is attributed to Berezin and Kac ``from Kyiv''. No triangularization statement is written.
statement: Over characteristic zero, finite-dimensional Lie superalgebras correspond to formal supergroup laws, with homomorphisms respected. This is a local/formal Lie correspondence; it does not assert that every representation of a solvable Lie superalgebra can be triangularized.
reconstruction: The identity of Kac is G. I. Kac, coauthor of the 1970 article, rather than an automatic identification with V. G. Kac. The theorem is interpreted using that precise paper.
fate: \citet[Section 3.5, Theorem 4]{berezinkac1970lie} proves the mutually inverse functors. This is an exact and pre-existing match to the attributed Lie correspondence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Gelfand’s nilpotent Taylor formula
notes: Gelfand writes \(p(t+\xi)=p(t)+p'(t)\xi\).
statement: For a polynomial \(p\) over a characteristic-zero commutative coefficient ring and a commuting nilpotent element \(\xi\) with \(\xi^2=0\), the binomial formula gives \(p(t+\xi)=p(t)+p'(t)\xi\). The same finite Taylor substitution is meaningful for smooth superfunctions with nilpotent increments. If \(t\) is even and \(\xi\) odd, this substitution by itself is not a parity-preserving even-coordinate change.
fate: The identity is elementary; the parity qualification separates the algebraic Taylor example from the preceding definition of supermanifold morphism.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Deformation in the direction of a super-Poisson bracket
notes: The notes end by asking to find deformations of the function superalgebra in the direction of its Poisson bracket.
statement: A precise even-bracket interpretation asks for an associative parity-preserving product \(f*g=fg+\sum_{r\ge1}\hbar^rB_r(f,g)\) such that the first graded commutator is \(\hbar\{f,g\}+O(\hbar^2)\). For a split smooth supermanifold built from a symplectic base and a vector bundle with a nondegenerate symmetric fibre metric, the associated Rothstein even super-Poisson bracket has such a differential star product.
reconstruction: Parity of the bracket, formal versus convergent deformation and nondegeneracy are absent from the notebook. The stated theorem is a definite later answer to an explicitly restricted interpretation, not a claim that all possible readings were equivalent.
fate: \citet[Theorems 1.3--1.4 and Corollary 1.1]{bordemann2000superpoisson}, first circulated on 30 March 2000, constructs the star product and identifies its first bracket. Odd brackets require a different formulation and are not covered by this identification.
present_status: As of November 2026, the stated even symplectic interpretation is solved; the notes do not specify a unique more general problem.

title: The row transfer matrix for the Ising model
notes: Rows are vectors \(x,y\in\{\pm1\}^n\), and \(A(x,y)=\exp\{\beta[J_1\sum x_ix_{i-1}+J_2\sum x_iy_i]\}\), with periodic indices.
statement: For an \(n\times R\) torus with nearest-neighbour horizontal and vertical couplings and no external field, the partition function is \(Z_{n,R}=\operatorname{tr}(A_n^R)\). Assigning all horizontal interactions to the first row produces the nonsymmetric matrix in the notes; splitting them equally gives a similar symmetric matrix. Each bond must be counted once.
fate: The finite-width transfer-operator problem is solved in \citet[Sections II--V]{onsager1944crystal}, received 4 October 1943 and published in 1944. The identity \(Z=\operatorname{tr}A^R\) follows immediately by summing cyclic row sequences.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Free energy and the thermodynamic limit
notes: The probability is proportional to \(e^{-\beta H}\), and the notes identify free energy through \(\lim R^{-2}\log Z\), with singularities associated with the dominant eigenvalue.
statement: For a finite system the Gibbs probability is \(e^{-\beta H}/Z\). At fixed width \(n\), positivity gives \(\lim_{R\to\infty}R^{-1}\log Z_{n,R}=\log\lambda_{\max}(A_n)\). A two-dimensional pressure requires a further width limit, or a joint limit with both side lengths tending to infinity. Finite positive transfer matrices have a simple dominant eigenvalue analytic in finite real couplings; a phase singularity arises only in an infinite-size limit.
reconstruction: The source uses the word free energy for the dimensionless pressure; physical free energy per site is its negative divided by \(\beta\). The distinction between fixed width and a two-dimensional limit is essential.
fate: \citet[abstract and Section IX]{onsager1944crystal} explicitly separates finite strips from the infinite crystal. The normalization here is fixed by the elementary Gibbs definition.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Onsager’s zero-field Ising solution
notes: The eigenvalues of the transfer matrix are attributed to Onsager, with a singularity at a distinguished temperature.
statement: For the infinite anisotropic square-lattice Ising ferromagnet with \(J_1,J_2>0\) and zero magnetic field, the critical inverse temperature is characterized by \(\sinh(2\beta_cJ_1)\sinh(2\beta_cJ_2)=1\). The exact free energy is nonanalytic there; the internal energy is continuous and the specific heat has a logarithmic divergence.
fate: These conclusions are in the original \citet[abstract and Section IX]{onsager1944crystal}. No statement about a nonzero magnetic field is warranted by the notes.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Anticommuting operators in the transfer-matrix solution
notes: Operators \(A_i\) anticommute and the transfer matrix is written schematically as \(\exp(\sum c_{ij}A_iA_j)\).
statement: A Clifford algebra organizes the zero-field transfer calculation. For periodic spin boundary conditions, fermion-parity sectors must be treated separately, and a scalar normalization may multiply the exponential of a quadratic Clifford expression. One should not read the schematic equality as a global sector-free normal form for every transfer matrix.
fate: The underlying algebra appears in \citet[Sections IV--VII]{onsager1944crystal}. The notebook compresses normalization and boundary-sector information, so the publication match is structural rather than a literal equality.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Lieb’s entropy of square ice
notes: Lieb is credited with finding the entropy for a model of ice.
statement: For the equal-weight square-ice model, each vertex has two incoming and two outgoing arrows. In the thermodynamic limit its number of states per vertex is \(W=(4/3)^{3/2}\), giving entropy per vertex \(k_B\log W\). This identifies the two-dimensional six-vertex model; it is not an exact entropy formula for three-dimensional physical ice.
fate: The detailed result is \citet[abstract and final entropy formula]{lieb1967squareice}, published on 5 October 1967 after a shorter April announcement. The original full text is a source target; publisher metadata and the result stated in the abstract are verified.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: The spectral curve and joint-eigenfunction sheaf
notes: For commuting scalar ordinary differential operators \(L_1,L_2\), the joint eigenvalues satisfy \(P(E_1,E_2)=0\). Coprime orders give a line bundle; orders four and six suggest a rank-two bundle.
statement: A commutative ring \(\mathcal A\) of ordinary scalar differential operators of positive order has an algebraic spectral curve, with a distinguished point at infinity. In the generic smooth case, common eigenspaces define a vector bundle of rank \(r\), the greatest common divisor of the orders of all nonzero operators in \(\mathcal A\). Coprime orders force \(r=1\); the gcd of a selected pair need not equal the rank of a larger ring.
reconstruction: The hypotheses are local smooth/analytic coefficients with nonvanishing leading coefficients, followed by a suitable normalization; singular spectral curves require torsion-free sheaves. The source's two selected orders do not by themselves fix the rank of every containing ring.
fate: \citet[Theorem 1.1 and Section 1]{krichever1978commutative} recalls the pre-existing spectral-curve construction and clarifies the spectral data. The 1978 paper distinguishes this direct construction from the inverse problem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Counting eigenvectors over a fixed spectral value
notes: After saying that the coprime case is one-dimensional, the notes say that the number of common eigenfunctions is \(n\), with distinct eigenvalues.
statement: If \(\operatorname{ord}L_1=n\), then \(\ker(L_1-E_1)\) is locally \(n\)-dimensional. The commuting \(L_2\) acts on this space. For generic \(E_1\) and rank one, it has \(n\) distinct eigenvalues, each with a one-dimensional joint eigenspace. Thus there are \(n\) points above a generic \(E_1\), not an \(n\)-dimensional eigenspace at one point \((E_1,E_2)\).
reconstruction: This separates the degree of the spectral projection from the rank of the eigenfunction bundle, resolving the apparent contradiction on the page.
fate: The solution-space construction used in the proof of \citet[Theorem 1.1]{krichever1978commutative} supplies precisely this distinction.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: The higher-rank inverse construction
notes: The inverse problem is explicitly marked ``not done'', with orders four and six as the rank-two example: construct commuting differential operators from the bundle.
statement: Given an appropriate smooth pointed spectral curve, rank-\(r\) bundle data, a local parameter and a compatible framing/asymptotic prescription at the marked point, reconstruct a commutative ring of scalar ordinary differential operators. A bare bundle without this extra data is not sufficient. In generic position, rank \(r\) also involves \(r-1\) functions of the independent variable after normalization.
fate: \citet[Theorem 2.3]{krichever1978commutative}, submitted 15 February 1977 and published in 1978, completes the generic smooth-curve construction. Its introduction expressly corrects errors in the 1977 implementation. This is a subsequent answer under stated generic hypotheses, not an unrestricted classification of all singular cases.
present_status: As of November 2026, the generic inverse correspondence described here is established; the notebook’s unrestricted shorthand must retain the spectral-data qualifications.

title: Drinfeld’s functional parameters and gauge normalization
notes: Drinfeld says \(d=(m,n)\) leaves \(d-1\) arbitrary functions; conjugation removes one coefficient, while a leading coefficient remains. Powers \(Q^2,Q^3\) already give order-four/order-six examples with two functions.
statement: After local change of independent variable and scalar conjugation, a monic order-\(r\) auxiliary operator can be normalized to \(\partial^r+v_{r-2}(x)\partial^{r-2}+\cdots+v_0(x)\), leaving \(r-1\) functions. Spectral curve and bundle parameters remain in addition. For an arbitrary order-two \(Q=a_2\partial^2+a_1\partial+a_0\), scalar conjugation can remove the first-order term locally; if coordinate changes are not also factored out, \(a_2\) remains alongside the potential.
reconstruction: The phrase ``specifying a pair iff specifying functions'' suppresses finite-dimensional spectral data and the equivalence relation. The example \(Q^2,Q^3\) explains why the choice of normalization matters.
fate: The normalized \(r-1\)-function statement is made precise by \citet[Theorem 2.3]{krichever1978commutative}. It applies to the ring rank, not automatically to the gcd of any chosen pair in a larger ring.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.
speaker: V. G. Drinfeld

title: Laplacian convention and Weyl frequencies
notes: Shnirelman takes a compact analytic Riemannian manifold, writes \(\Delta u_k+\lambda_k^2u_k=0\), defines \(\Delta\) through spherical averages, and invokes \(\lambda_k\sim c k^{1/n}\).
statement:
Let \(M\) be a closed smooth Riemannian \(n\)-manifold and use the nonpositive Laplace--Beltrami operator. Then \(-\Delta u_k=\lambda_k^2u_k\), with \(\lambda_k\ge0\), counted with multiplicity. Weyl's law is
\[N(\Lambda)\sim\frac{\omega_n\operatorname{Vol}(M)}{(2\pi)^n}\Lambda^n.\]
For normalized averages over small geodesic spheres, \(\Delta f=2n\lim_{\tau\to0}(\operatorname{avg}_{S_\tau}f-f)/\tau^2\).
reconstruction: Closedness supplies the missing boundary hypothesis. The factor \(2n\) is obtained by a normal-coordinate Taylor expansion. Analyticity is stronger than needed for the Weyl law.
fate: The relevant positive elliptic spectral setting already appears in \citet[opening hypotheses]{duistermaatguillemin1975spectrum}; the sphere normalization is reconstructed directly. Publication metadata, rather than the original full proof, was read.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.
speaker: A. I. Shnirelman

title: The rectangular flat-torus spectrum
notes: The example uses a flat torus and frequencies \(\lambda^2=n^2/a^2+m^2/b^2\); one displayed eigenvalue equation reverses the earlier sign of \(\Delta\).
statement: On \(\mathbb R^2/(2\pi a\mathbb Z\times2\pi b\mathbb Z)\), the functions \(e^{i(nx/a+my/b)}\) have eigenvalues \(n^2/a^2+m^2/b^2\) for \(-\Delta\). Multiplicities and the zero mode must be retained when listing the frequencies. The positive-sign equation is for \(-\Delta\), not the previously defined \(\Delta\).
fate: This is an elementary separation-of-variables calculation. It supplies a test case for the spectral-phase question, but its highly degenerate closed geodesics do not satisfy the later isolated-orbit hypotheses.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.
speaker: A. I. Shnirelman

title: Abel-renormalized distributions of spectral phases
notes: The question concerns \(a\lambda_k\pmod{2\pi}\). The proposed distribution subtracts its constant Fourier mode and multiplies an exponentially smoothed spectral sum by \(\varepsilon\).
statement:
Let \((M,g)\) be a closed compact Riemannian manifold, and let \(\lambda_k\ge0\) be the eigenvalues of \(\sqrt{-\Delta_g}\), counted with multiplicity. With \(\delta_{\rm per}\) the periodic delta distribution and \(a>0\), define
\[\Phi_{a,\varepsilon}(\mu)=\varepsilon\sum_k e^{-\varepsilon\lambda_k}\left(\delta_{\rm per}(\mu-a\lambda_k)-\frac1{2\pi}\right).\]
Ask whether \(\Phi_{a,\varepsilon}\) has a limit in \(\mathcal D'(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)\), and how its Fourier coefficients depend on closed geodesics. This is a signed renormalized distribution, not the probability distribution of the first \(N\) phases. The notebook's intended generic setting has isolated closed geodesics with pairwise incommensurable primitive unoriented lengths; nondegeneracy of every contributing iterate is an additional modern hypothesis needed for the quoted principal trace formula.
reconstruction: The precise topology and the sign convention in the Fourier transform are supplied here. The \(m\ne0\) coefficient is \(\varepsilon(2\pi)^{-1}\operatorname{tr}e^{-(\varepsilon+ima)\sqrt{-\Delta}}\); its individual limit and distributional convergence are different questions. The exclusion of iterates and orientation reversal from the incommensurability assertion is necessary: otherwise that assumption is impossible. The source's nondegeneracy abbreviation is not deciphered with certainty.
fate: The closed-orbit interpretation is supported by the wave-trace expansion, already developed in 1975 and explicitly recalled by \citet[Introduction]{zelditch1998wave}. No located source proves the entire global distributional assertion in exactly the notebook's generality. The chapter supplies a precise Fourier convergence criterion, the complete circle calculation and a sphere example outside the generic assumptions; it does not establish the general geometric limit.
present_status: As of November 2026, the fixed-Fourier-mode interpretation is identified; a theorem with sufficient uniform bounds for the notebook’s full Abel limit was not located in the targeted searches.
worth: Uniform control of all Fourier modes is the remaining analytical step; the bounded circle model and the degenerate sphere example clarify the necessary scope.
speaker: A. I. Shnirelman

title: Closed-geodesic resonances in spectral phases
notes: Under a genericity assumption, the notes say \(\Phi_a\ne0\) precisely when \(a\) is a rational multiple of a closed-geodesic length.
statement: At a fixed nonzero Fourier index \(m\), a possible contribution occurs when \(|m|a\) is a closed-orbit length. For finitely many isolated nondegenerate orbits of that length, the leading coefficient is a sum of their principal wave invariants. Nonvanishing requires this sum not to cancel. ``Distinct incommensurable lengths'' can only refer to primitive unoriented geodesics: iterates and orientation reversal already force relations.
reconstruction: This is a justified local interpretation of the resonance statement. It does not assert a global distributional ``if and only if'' without the convergence and noncancellation hypotheses of the preceding item.
fate: The singularities and their orbital coefficients belong to the pre-existing wave-trace theory; \citet[Introduction]{zelditch1998wave}. The exact Shnirelman publication for this Abel formulation remains unidentified.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.
speaker: A. I. Shnirelman

title: The symplectic return map and its spectral types
notes: A closed geodesic has a Poincaré map; its multipliers are listed as reciprocal real pairs, unit-circle pairs, and complex quadruples, with the last type associated with dimension three.
statement: The linearized return map acts symplectically on a transverse space of dimension \(2n-2\). Its nonreal, non-unit multipliers occur in quadruples \(\lambda,\bar\lambda,\lambda^{-1},\bar\lambda^{-1}\); real and unit-circle pairs give hyperbolic and elliptic blocks. A quadruple requires \(n\ge3\), not \(n=3\) exclusively. Nondegeneracy at an iterate means \(\det(I-P_\gamma^k)\ne0\).
fate: The block decomposition and nondegenerate setting are used in \citet[Section 1]{zelditch1998wave}. The reciprocal-pair assertion also follows directly from symplectic linear algebra.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.
speaker: A. I. Shnirelman

title: Elliptic and hyperbolic orbit amplitudes
notes: The coefficients are written with denominators \(\sin(k\alpha/2)\), \(\sinh(k\alpha/2)\), and \((-1)^k/\sinh(k\alpha/2)\) for three multiplier types.
statement: The magnitude of a nondegenerate block's contribution is proportional to \(|\det(I-P^k)|^{-1/2}\), with a separate Maslov phase. For multipliers \(e^{\pm i\alpha}\) it is \((2|\sin(k\alpha/2)|)^{-1}\); for \(e^{\pm\alpha}\), \((2|\sinh(k\alpha/2)|)^{-1}\). For \(-e^{\pm\alpha}\), even \(k\) gives the hyperbolic sine denominator, while odd \(k\) gives \(2\cosh(k\alpha/2)\).
reconstruction: \ours\ These three magnitudes are obtained directly by multiplying \((1-\lambda^k)(1-\lambda^{-k})\). A factor \((-1)^k\) cannot replace the sine/cosine distinction in the negative-real case.
fate: The determinant and phase organization is the metaplectic form recalled in \citet[Introduction, equation (0.1)]{zelditch1998wave}. The block calculation corrects the literal manuscript formula.

title: Regularizing the elliptic delta comb
notes: A regularized sum of deltas at half-integer multiples of an angle is written with the damping factor and constant subtraction inside the argument of \(\delta\). The preceding line explicitly requires the angle to be poorly approximable by rationals.
statement:
One coherent reconstruction is
\[D_{\alpha,\varepsilon}=\sum_{r\ge0}e^{-\varepsilon r}\left(\delta_{\rm per}(\mu-(r+\tfrac12)\alpha)-\frac1{2\pi}\right).\]
For \(m\ne0\), its Fourier coefficient is \((2\pi)^{-1}e^{-im\alpha/2}/(1-e^{-\varepsilon-im\alpha})\). If \(|1-e^{-im\alpha}|^{-1}\) grows at most polynomially, these coefficients converge to a distribution; a Diophantine condition on \(\alpha/2\pi\) suffices. Irrationality alone does not supply that bound.
reconstruction: \ours\ The placement of damping and subtraction is emended to make a standard Abel sum. The Fourier coefficients follow from a geometric series and show exactly where a small-divisor hypothesis enters. The notebook does supply a poor-approximation hypothesis; the polynomial Fourier bound makes its required role precise.
fate: The stated regularization and convergence criterion are derived here directly. No exact publication match to the manuscript’s misplaced parentheses was found.

title: Hyperbolic continuation and an elliptic-function sketch
notes: The hyperbolic case is illustrated with poles and a reference to a Weierstrass function, but period and scale normalizations are not recorded.
statement: A hyperbolic-block sequence has exponentially decaying coefficients such as \(1/\sinh(k\alpha/2)\). It therefore defines a periodic analytic function in a nonzero complex strip. A meromorphic expression in terms of elliptic functions would additionally require its periods, residues and additive normalization.
fate: The sketch does not identify a unique Weierstrass function or an exact identity. Searches on Shnirelman, spectral phases, hyperbolic multipliers and Weierstrass functions did not recover that identity.

title: Holomorphic half-wave trace versus meromorphic continuation
notes: For \(f(z)=\sum e^{i\lambda_kz}\), the notes claim downward analytic continuation with simple poles at geodesic lengths and identify residues with Fourier coefficients.
statement: For \(\operatorname{Im}z>0\), the sum converges normally on compact subsets by Weyl's bound. Its boundary value is the distributional half-wave trace. At an isolated nondegenerate nonzero closed-orbit length, its leading singularity has simple-pole type, but lower terms generally include powers times logarithms. At zero the leading singularity has order \(n\). These facts do not yield global meromorphic continuation through the real axis.
fate: The singularity expansion in \citet[Introduction, first displayed formula]{zelditch1998wave} contains the logarithmic terms absent from the notebook. This continues the wave-trace discussion of occurrences 1973-333.18--20.

title: Sturm’s bound for linear combinations
notes: The discussion recalls a one-dimensional bound on the zeros of a linear combination of the first eigenfunctions and compares it with polynomials.
statement: For a regular real Sturm--Liouville problem on a compact interval with separated self-adjoint boundary conditions, order the simple eigenvalues increasingly. A nonzero linear combination of eigenfunctions with indices \(m,\ldots,n\) has at least \(m-1\) sign changes and at most \(n-1\) interior zeros, with multiplicities treated in the precise Sturm version. In particular the span of the first \(n\) eigenfunctions is a Chebyshev space in the interior.
fate: The original theorem was announced in 1833 and published in 1836. A modern proof is \citet[Theorems 1.4 and2.15]{berardhelffer2018sturm}: first circulated 26 June 2017, revised16 October 2018, and published in the 2020 journal issue. The distinction between circulation and issue year is retained.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Courant’s nodal-domain bound
notes: The multidimensional comparison invokes the bound for an individual Laplace eigenfunction.
statement: For a real eigenfunction associated to the \(n\)-th eigenvalue of a self-adjoint Laplacian on a connected compact manifold, or a bounded domain with standard Dirichlet or Neumann conditions, the number of nodal domains is at most \(n\), with eigenvalues counted with multiplicity. This theorem applies to a single eigenspace; it does not automatically extend to sums of different eigenvalues.
fate: The classical theorem and indexing convention are restated in \citet[Theorem 1.1]{berardhelffer2018courant}. The distinction from an extended assertion is the issue raised in the next intervention.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Arnold’s Harnack-type question for eigenfunction sums
notes: Arnold asks about transferring Harnack-type assertions to linear combinations of eigenfunctions. No precise numerical bound is recorded.
statement: A natural definite comparison is the extended Courant property: a nonzero sum of eigenfunctions with eigenvalues at most \(\lambda_n\) should have no more nodal domains than the first index of \(\lambda_n\). This property is false in general. For example, the Neumann equilateral triangle admits a constant plus a second eigenfunction with three nodal domains, exceeding the first index two.
reconstruction: The extended Courant property is an explicit reconstruction of one plausible Harnack-type question, not a verbatim conjecture of Arnold in these notes. Other algebraic-geometric bounds may remain meaningful.
fate: \citet[Statement 1.2 and Section 3]{berardhelffer2018courant}, circulated in 2017 and published in 2018, gives this precise comparison and counterexample. It does not settle every unspecified Harnack-type inequality.
present_status: As of November 2026, the specified extended Courant assertion is disproved. The general wording in the seminar is broader and cannot be assigned that single fate without the reconstruction caveat.

title: Ground-state positivity and the polynomial analogy
notes: The first eigenfunction is described as positive everywhere; successive eigenfunctions are compared with a linear function and a conic before the nodal-set questions.
statement: For the scalar Laplacian on a connected closed manifold the lowest eigenvalue is zero and its eigenfunctions are constant, so a ground state can be chosen strictly positive. For a connected bounded domain with Dirichlet conditions, the first eigenfunction is strictly positive in the interior after choosing its sign, and vanishes on the boundary. The comparisons of later eigenfunctions with linear and quadratic polynomials are an analogy, not a general classification of their nodal sets.
reconstruction: Connectedness, the boundary condition and the choice of sign are supplied; ``everywhere'' must be restricted to the interior in the Dirichlet case.
fate: This is the standard ground-state comparison underlying the nodal discussion; \citet[Introduction and Theorem 1.1]{berardhelffer2018courant}. The later-eigenfunction analogy does not add a theorem beyond the precise Sturm and Courant assertions.

title: Continuum action and its coupling convention
notes: The action is \((4e^2)^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\int A_{\mu\nu}^2\), immediately followed by a definition of \(F_{\mu\nu}\); the commutator has no coupling constant.
statement:
After absorbing the coupling into the connection, \(F=dA+A\wedge A\) and \(S_E=-(4e^2)^{-1}\int\operatorname{tr}F_{\mu
u}F_{\mu
u}\,d^4x\) for anti-Hermitian matrices. Stationarity gives \(D^\mu F_{\mu
u}=0\). If the matrices commute, the curvature reduces to the Abelian electromagnetic expression.
reconstruction: The curvature symbol in the integrand and Euclidean sign are emended; the changed coupling convention is legitimate. The Euler--Lagrange equation assumes compactly supported variations or vanishing boundary terms.
fate: This is the continuum starting point for \citet[Sections I--II]{wilson1974confinement}, already published in 1974.

title: Link variables and plaquette action
notes: Each directed link carries \(B_{x,\mu}\in SU(2)\); the four-link plaquette product enters a class function \(\chi\), called ``any character'' and then described as constant on conjugacy classes.
statement:
For link variables \(U_{x,\mu}\), set
\[U_p=U_{x,\mu}U_{x+a_\mu,
u}U^{-1}_{x+a_
u,\mu}U^{-1}_{x,
u}.\]
Under \(U_{x,\mu}\mapsto\Omega_x^{-1}U_{x,\mu}\Omega_{x+a_\mu}\), the plaquette is conjugated at \(x\). Hence \(\sum_p\phi(U_p)\) is gauge invariant for every class function \(\phi\). A character is a special class function. The Wilson choice is proportional to \(\sum_p(1- rac12\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}U_p)\).
reconstruction: An arbitrary class function gives an invariant lattice action but does not automatically have the desired continuum Yang--Mills limit. The subtraction and small-plaquette quadratic normalization distinguish the Wilson choice.
fate: The link and plaquette construction is \citet[Section III]{wilson1974confinement}, received 12 June 1974 and published 15 October 1974. The source is therefore expository, not a new 1976 discretization.

title: Finite-lattice Haar integral and correlations
notes: The notes write \(Z=\int\prod_{x,\mu}dB_{x,\mu}e^{-S(B)}\), count \(4n\) group integrations and \(12n\) variables, and leave a heading for correlation functions.
statement: On a finite periodic four-dimensional lattice with \(n\) sites, there are \(4n\) independent positively oriented links. Normalized Haar measure on each \(SU(2)\) factor defines \(Z\); for a real continuous action, \(0<Z<\infty\). Expectations are \(\langle O\rangle=Z^{-1}\int Oe^{-S}\prod dU\). The unreduced configuration space has dimension \(12n\); the quotient by gauge transformations does not have that dimension.
fate: \citet[Section III]{wilson1974confinement} provides the gauge-invariant lattice integral. Existence at finite lattice spacing and volume follows from compactness and does not establish an infinite-volume or continuum limit.

title: Wick rotation and the continuum functional integral
notes: The schematic replacement \(t\to it\), \(e^{iS}\to e^{-S}\), is followed by ``in the continuous case---a functional integral''. No measure is constructed.
statement: Imaginary-time continuation motivates the Euclidean Boltzmann factor after the action and integration contour are transformed consistently. title: The Hamiltonian cochain complex in polynomial symbols
notes: The opening calls the algebra formal divergence-free vector fields, then writes alternating polynomials in pairs \((\xi_i,\eta_i)\), with differential built from \(\langle\xi_i,\eta_j\rangle-\langle\xi_j,\eta_i\rangle\).
statement:
The displayed complex is the continuous Chevalley--Eilenberg complex of
\[\mathfrak{ham}_{2n}=\mathbb R[[p_1,\ldots,p_n,q_1,\ldots,q_n]]/\mathbb R\]
with the Poisson bracket. A cochain is represented by a polynomial alternating under exchange of argument pairs and vanishing when any entire pair is zero. Writing \(z_i=(\xi_i,\eta_i)\) and \(\omega(z_i,z_j)=\langle\xi_i,\eta_j\rangle-\langle\xi_j,\eta_i\rangle\), the source convention is
\[(dP)(z_1,\ldots,z_{q+1})=\sum_{i<j}(-1)^{i+j-1}\omega(z_i,z_j)P(z_i+z_j,z_1,\ldots,\widehat z_i,\ldots,\widehat z_j,\ldots,z_{q+1}).\]
The order of the remaining arguments is unchanged.
reconstruction: The quotient by constants supplies the omitted reduced-cochain condition. In two variables divergence-free formal fields are Hamiltonian; in higher even dimension the two Lie algebras differ. The Poisson factor, not the opening shorthand, identifies this complex.
fate: The algebra and continuous weight convention are explicitly fixed in \citet[Section 2]{kotschickmorita2009gkf}. The displayed differential is the dual of the Poisson bracket, so its square is zero by Jacobi.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Computing the full Hamiltonian cohomology
notes: The underlined task is to find the cohomology of the displayed complex, said to remain undone even for \(n=1\).
statement: Determine the continuous cohomology \(H^*(\mathfrak{ham}_{2n};\mathbb R)\), including its graded dimensions and multiplicative structure. The first unresolved case intended here is \(\mathfrak{ham}_2\), not the Lie algebra of all formal vector fields in one variable.
fate: Later computations and factorizations give substantial finite-weight information. \citet[p.151 and Theorem 1.2]{mikami2016metoki} still states the infinite-dimensionality question and proves the Metoki-class factorization. Stable-rank graph-homology calculations concern a different limiting object \citep[Remark 2.1]{moritasakasaisuzuki2015computations}.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, targeted searches located no complete fixed-rank computation or resolution of the infinitude question. The latest explicitly verified open-status statement used here is from 2016; this search result is not a proof of present-day nonexistence.
worth: The finite weight complexes permit exact calculations, but a full answer needs a mechanism valid in unbounded weights.

title: The all-vector-field comparison
notes: The notes say that taking polynomials linear in \(\eta\) gives the cochain complex of \(W_n\).
statement: Fibre-linear Hamiltonians \(H_v(p,q)=\sum_i p_i v_i(q)\) form a Lie subalgebra isomorphic, up to the fixed Poisson-sign convention, to the Lie algebra \(W_n\) of formal vector fields on \(\mathbb R^n\). Restricting Hamiltonian cochains to this subalgebra retains the symbol component linear in each fibre variable. This is a restriction map of complexes; those polynomial components need not form a subcomplex of the unrestricted Hamiltonian-symbol complex without projection.
reconstruction: The restriction interpretation makes the informal sentence precise and prevents the next sentence, ``not done even for \(n=1\)'', from being misapplied to \(W_1\).
fate: The cohomology of \(W_n\) had already been calculated by \citet[Theorem 0.3]{gelfandfuchs1970formal}, received 4 November 1969 and published in 1970. The full original English article was opened; the present distinction follows from the displayed fibre-linear embedding.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Finite bigraded complexes and off-diagonal contraction
notes: The total degrees in \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) are \(m_1+q\) and \(m_2+q\). Each \(K_{m_1,m_2}\) is finite-dimensional, and \(m_1\ne m_2\) is acyclic.
statement:
The differential preserves the two shifted degrees. For fixed \(n,m_1,m_2\), only finitely many exterior monomials occur: the weight-minus-one translation space is finite-dimensional, the quadratic weight-zero space is finite-dimensional, and every other factor has positive weight. The Hamiltonian \(\sum_i p_iq_i\) acts on this complex by the scalar \(m_1-m_2\), up to sign. Cartan's identity gives a contracting homotopy on a nonzero eigenspace, hence
\[H^*(\mathfrak{ham}_{2n})=\bigoplus_m H^*(K_{m,m}).\]
reconstruction: \ours\ The finiteness argument and contraction are supplied explicitly. The formal-cochain topology is continuous cohomology; an unrestricted algebraic dual would be a different object.
fate: The finite weight construction agrees with \citet[Section 2]{kotschickmorita2009gkf}. The source already states the reduction; the argument here explains why it is valid.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Low weights and the exotic Gelfand–Kalinin–Fuchs classes
notes: For \(n=1\), the notes give acyclicity at \(m=1,2,3\) and nonzero cohomology in degrees 7 and 10 at \(m=4\), followed by a machine-memory failure at \(m=5\).
statement: In total Hamiltonian weight \(w=2m\), the exotic relative Gelfand--Kalinin--Fuchs class lies in \(H^7(\mathfrak{ham}_2,\mathfrak{sp}_2)_8\). The corresponding absolute complex has classes in degrees 7 and 10. The statement about exhausted computer memory is a report about a calculation, not a cohomological vanishing or nonvanishing assertion. The absolute complexes at weights \(2,4,6\) are acyclic.
fate: The exotic class was published in Russian in 1972. Its later factorization is recalled in \citet[Theorem 1.1]{mikami2016metoki}: a degree-five, weight-ten class for fields vanishing at the origin is multiplied by the transverse symplectic class. Theorem 1.2 similarly factors the Metoki class of degree nine and weight fourteen, first reported in 1999.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Relative cohomology and the omitted zero-weight exception
notes: A subcomplex \(K'_{m,m}\) is introduced with \(H(K_{m,m})=H(K'_{m,m})\otimes H(S^3)\); its Euler characteristic is initially denoted \(\chi_m^*\), then loses the star.
statement:
Here \(K'\) is relative to quadratic Hamiltonians \(\mathfrak{sp}_2\cong\mathfrak{sl}_2\). For \(m\ne0\),
\[H^q(K_{m,m})\cong H^q(K'_{m,m})\oplus H^{q-3}(K'_{m,m}).\]
At weight zero, absolute groups occur in degrees0 and7, relative groups in degrees0 and4. The nontrivial Euler series is therefore relative; the absolute Euler characteristics vanish.
fate: The zero-weight exception is explicit in \citet[Section 1 and Theorem 2.1]{mohammadzadehfuchs2014cohomology}.

title: Perchik’s constant-term Euler series
notes: Perchik is credited with a generating function whose constant term in \(x\) is \(t^{-2}+2-t^8-t^{14}-t^{22}+\cdots+10t^{70}+\cdots\). The general row of factors contains an ambiguous middle exponent of \(t\).
statement:
Put \(E_m=\chi H^*(\mathfrak{ham}_2,\mathfrak{sp}_2)_{2m}\). Then
\[\sum_{m\ge-1}E_mt^{2m}=\frac12\operatorname{CT}_x\left[(1-t^{-1}x^{-1})(1-t^{-1}x)(1-x^{-2})(1-x^2)\prod_{\ell\ge1}\prod_{j=0}^{\ell+2}(1-t^\ell x^{-\ell-2+2j})\right].\]
The infinite product has a well-defined formal Laurent expansion in \(t\) with lower bound \(-2\). The linear Hamiltonians supply the two negative-weight factors; deleting them gives a different Lie algebra, \(\mathfrak{ham}_2^0\).
reconstruction: The symbol \(\operatorname{CT}_x\) formalizes ``discard everything containing \(x\)''. Every factor in the weight-\(\ell\) row has \(t^\ell\). Section~\ref{dev:perchik} gives an independent invariant-character derivation and finite cutoff proof.
fate: Harvard's dissertation list dates Perchik's dissertation to 1975 \citep{perchik1975dissertation}; this documents earlier work, but neither a precise public-availability date nor a theorem locator in the dissertation was verified. The expository classification E is therefore provisional, based on that documented dissertation; exact pre-seminar public circulation remains unestablished. The article appeared in 1976. \citet[Section 5]{kotschickmorita2009gkf} distinguishes the relative constructions; its Remark 9 has an inconsistent superscript for the full series, which is not followed here.
present_status: As of November 2026, the relative constant-term formula is established in the later primary literature; its exact pre-seminar circulation remains unverified.

title: Infinitely many nonzero relative Euler characteristics
notes: Fuchs asks to prove that \(\chi_m\ne0\) for arbitrarily large \(m\). The question follows the relative-complex notation and Perchik's product.
statement: For the coefficients \(E_m\) of the preceding fixed-rank relative Euler series, prove or disprove that \(\{m\ge1:E_m\ne0\}\) is infinite. A positive answer implies infinitely many nonzero weight components of Hamiltonian cohomology; the converse does not follow, since even and odd cohomology can cancel in an Euler characteristic.
fate: The exact coefficient-infinitude question persists in \citet[Section 2]{mohammadzadehfuchs2014cohomology}. The weaker cohomology-infinitude question remains explicit in \citet[p.151]{mikami2016metoki}. This chapter establishes only a finite truncation and exact coefficient verification.
present_status: As of 10 November 2026, no resolution of this exact coefficient-infinitude question was located in the recorded targeted searches. The chapter’s computation through m=150 supplies finite evidence and no claim about all later weights.
worth: A closed asymptotic or structural argument for the constant-term series would turn finite evidence into an infinitude theorem.

title: The numerical lower bound of 57 cohomology classes
notes: The expansion through \(t^{70}\) is said to prove the existence of at least 57 nontrivial cohomology classes.
statement:
For each finite relative weight complex, \(\sum_q\dim H^q_{2m}\ge|E_m|\). The computed coefficients satisfy
\[\sum_{m=-1}^{35}|E_m|=57.\]
Thus the total relative cohomology has dimension at least 57 when these weights, including weight zero and the negative weight, are included. The positive weights alone give 54. The number does not mean 57 positive-weight primitive exotic generators.
reconstruction: \oursComputed\ The chapter independently reproduces this finite sum and \(E_{35}=10\), then extends the verified range through \(m=150\). The inequality is the elementary comparison of the alternating and ungraded dimensions of a finite complex.
fate: This supplies a precise interpretation and independent check of the notebook's 57. The development does not equate an Euler coefficient with a cohomological dimension or a count of algebra generators.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Multiplication dualized to a coproduct
notes: Buchstaber starts with \(X\times X\to X\) for a genuine group and writes a map \(C(X)\to C(X\times X)\) as a coalgebra structure.
statement: For a compact Hausdorff topological group, multiplication gives \(\Delta f(x,y)=f(xy)\) on continuous functions, with counit evaluation at the identity. Associativity gives coassociativity. In this setting \(C(X\times X)\) is a completed tensor product; an algebraic tensor-product coalgebra is obtained instead on a suitable algebra of representative functions.
reconstruction: The topology and tensor-product convention are supplied. Arbitrary continuous functions need not lie in the algebraic tensor product \(C(X)\otimes C(X)\).
fate: The algebra/coalgebra viewpoint leads directly into \citet[Section 3]{buchstaber1975twovaluedI}, received 2 December 1974 and published in 1975. The notebook gives only the opening construction, not a complete theorem about all topological spaces.

title: Averaging a two-valued formal multiplication
notes: The next line replaces a value of \(f(x\cdot y)\) by its mathematical expectation. The heading says that Buchstaber is reporting Adams on Buchstaber.
statement:
For a commutative two-valued formal group law over a \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra, with branches \(F_+(x,y),F_-(x,y)\), the natural linear coproduct is
\[\Delta f=\tfrac12\bigl(f(F_+(x,y))+f(F_-(x,y))\bigr).\]
The symmetric expression is interpreted through the formal law even when its branches are not separately in the base power-series ring. Associativity of the two-valued law gives coassociativity of this averaging map, which generally is not an algebra homomorphism.
reconstruction: This is a concrete, explicitly labelled identification of the expectation notation, supported by the contemporaneous two-valued-formal-group literature. The fragment does not itself specify the number of values or the full axioms.
fate: The construction is read in \citet[Section 3 and the generalized translations of Section 4]{buchstaber1975twovaluedI}. The bibliographical lead Adams--Liulevicius, ``Buhstaber's work on two-valued formal groups'' (1975), matches the heading, but its full text was not accessible and no detailed theorem is attributed to it here.

title: The Lorentz metric and proper time
notes: Coordinates are \((x^0,\vec x)=(ct,\vec x)\), the flat metric has diagonal entries \((1,-1,-1,-1)\), and proper time is called the length of a curve.
statement:
A spacetime is a smooth four-manifold with a Lorentz metric of signature \((+---)\). Along a future-directed timelike curve \(\gamma\),
\[\tau(\gamma)=c^{-1}\int\sqrt{g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)}\,ds.\]
Null curves have zero Lorentzian length. A proper-time interpretation therefore requires a timelike curve and includes the factor \(c^{-1}\) when \(x^0=ct\).
fate: The metric interpretation is classical; \citet[Sections 3--4]{einstein1916foundation}. The modern signature and units have been fixed explicitly.
present_status: As of November 2026, the reconstructed statement is standard.

title: Curvature contractions and Einstein’s equation
notes: The curvature is a two-form with values in the Lie algebra of \(O(n)\); contraction gives \(R_{ij}\) and \(R\). The field equation is \(R_{ij}-\tfrac12Rg_{ij}=(8\pi K/c^4)T_{ij}\), followed by its arbitrary-dimensional form.
statement: In a Lorentz-orthonormal frame, the curvature takes values in \(\mathfrak{o}(1,3)\), not \(\mathfrak{o}(4)\). Fix a curvature-sign convention and let \(R_{ij}=R^k{}_{ikj}\), \(R=g^{ij}R_{ij}\). With zero cosmological constant, Einstein's equation is \(G_{ij}=\kappa T_{ij}\), where \(G_{ij}=R_{ij}-\tfrac12Rg_{ij}\) and \(\kappa=8\pi G/c^4\). The tensor formula exists in any dimension, but in dimension two \(G\) vanishes identically.
reconstruction: The orthogonal Lie algebra is corrected for the displayed signature. The notes' historical date 1916 is the year of Einstein's systematic exposition, not the first formulation of the final field equation.
fate: The contractions and field equation appear in \citet[Sections 12, 14 and 16]{einstein1916foundation}. The exposition itself cites the 1915 work.

title: Stress–energy from variation of the metric
notes: The source writes \(S=\int L\sqrt g\,d^4x\) and \(\sqrt g\,T_{ij}=\delta S/\delta g_{ij}\).
statement:
For Lorentz signature the invariant density is \(\sqrt{|\det g|}\). One consistent convention is
\[\delta S_m=\frac12\int\sqrt{|g|}\,T_{ij}\,\delta g^{ij}\,d^4x
=-\frac12\int\sqrt{|g|}\,T^{ij}\,\delta g_{ij}\,d^4x.\]
Thus \(T_{ij}=2|g|^{-1/2}\delta S_m/\delta g^{ij}\) in this convention. Reversing the sign of the matter action reverses the defining sign; it does not remove the factor two or the change of index positions.
reconstruction: \ours\ The second equality follows by differentiating \(g^{ik}g_{kj}=\delta^i_j\). The sign convention is declared rather than inferred from the abbreviated notebook Lagrangian.
fate: This is a normalization of the standard variational definition. The notebook formula is mathematically incomplete as an indexed variational identity.

title: The electromagnetic action and differential form
notes: The electromagnetic Lagrangian is written \(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}\); the curvature two-form is written with reversed wedge indices and no half.
statement:
For a local potential one-form \(A\), set
\[F=dA=	frac12F_{\mu
u}\,dx^\mu\wedge dx^
u,\qquad F_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu.\]
With signature \((+---)\), choose \(L_m=-	frac14F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}\). The preceding variational convention gives \(T_{\mu
u}=-F_{\mu\alpha}F_
u{}^\alpha+	frac14g_{\mu
u}F_{\alpha eta}F^{\alpha eta}\), whose energy density in an orthonormal frame is \((|E|^2+|B|^2)/2\).
